sources.liguori: St Alphonsus Liguori, The Glories of Mary (1888)
sources.faber: Fr Frederick William Faber, The Foot of the Cross (1858)
sources.marmion: Bl Columba Marmion OSB, Christ in His Mysteries (1924)
sources.denis: Denis the Carthusian, Enarratio in Canticum Canticorum (1898), trans. from the Latin for Still

scripture.text: Then Jesus came with them into a country place which is called Gethsemani. And he said to his disciples: Sit you here, till I go yonder and pray.

meditations.body: Gethsemani means oil press — a working grove on the Mount of Olives where the fruit was crushed until it yielded. John adds a detail worth carrying into the decade: Judas knew the place, because Jesus often resorted there with His disciples. This was His habitual place of prayer. The betrayer's whole plan depended on the Lord's faithfulness to His nightly habit — and the Lord, knowing it, went anyway, at the usual hour, to the usual place.

scripture.text: Then he saith to them: My soul is sorrowful even unto death. Stay you here and watch with me.

meditations.body: The Maker of the stars tells three fishermen that He needs company.

scripture.text: And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. And being in an agony, he prayed the longer. And his sweat became as drops of blood, trickling down upon the ground.

meditations.body: Marmion refuses to soften the scene: for three hours, he says, weariness, sadness, sorrow and anguish sweep over His soul like a torrent, and take such possession of it that the blood escapes from His sacred veins. Notice what Luke says He did under that torrent. Not less prayer — He prayed the longer. The worse it became, the longer He stayed at it. That is the whole instruction of this mystery, given before a word of it is explained.

scripture.text: Saying: Father, if thou wilt, remove this chalice from me: but yet not my will, but thine be done.

meditations.body: Does the first half of that prayer mean Christ no longer accepts His Father's will? Marmion answers: certainly He accepts it. The plea to remove the chalice is the cry of the sensitive part of poor human nature crushed by weariness and suffering — at this moment He is above all the Man of Sorrows, a man acquainted with infirmity. And then Marmion adds the sentence that changes how you pray: He would have us know this, and therefore He thus prays. The recoil was allowed to speak on purpose, so that yours would have somewhere to go.

scripture.text: And going a little further, he fell upon his face, praying and saying: My Father, if it be possible, let this chalice pass from me. Nevertheless, not as I will but as thou wilt.

meditations.body: The second half of the prayer Marmion calls love's triumph. And he presses on a hard fact: the Father, had He so decreed, could have lessened the sufferings, could have changed the circumstances of that death. He did not so will. Did that diminish the Son's love? Marmion's answer is exact — He does not say, my Father might have arranged things otherwise. No accounting, no appeal to the version of the will of God He would have preferred. There is a way of accepting that keeps the ledger open. This is the other way.

scripture.text: And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. And being in an agony, he prayed the longer.

meditations.body: St Peter Chrysologus, in the citation Liguori preserves, sets this verse beside the Annunciation: as Christ willed to be strengthened by an angel, so the Virgin had to be encouraged by an angel. If you have prayed the Joyful mysteries with this app, you have met this parallel from the other side. Twice the same help is sent — once to a girl at the beginning, once to her Son at the end — because on both nights a human will was being asked for something enormous, and heaven does not despise the need for help in saying yes.

scripture.text: But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart.

meditations.body: Where was His mother that night? Asleep in a house in the city, so far as the body goes. But Faber holds that by a miraculous grace she assisted in spirit at the Agony — saw His Heart unveiled throughout, and felt in herself, according to her measure, a corresponding agony. Whether or not you follow him to the miracle, the pattern beneath it is certain and repeatable: those who have long pondered Christ in their hearts come to suffer with Him in the night hours, uninvited and unseen. Every adorer at a midnight holy hour since has been standing in her company.

scripture.text: And forthwith coming to Jesus, he said: Hail, Rabbi. And he kissed him.

meditations.body: Faber records something almost unbearable in one subordinate clause: she saw the treachery of Judas consummated, in spite of her intense prayers for that unhappy soul. Mary prayed for Judas. Intensely. And the prayer was not granted, because the soul it was offered for kept the freedom to refuse — the same wall her prayers would strike on Calvary with the second thief. If her intercession could be declined, yours can be too, and that is not evidence against praying. She did not stop. Neither should you, for whichever soul it is that you have almost given up asking about.

scripture.text: And he cometh to his disciples and findeth them asleep. And he saith to Peter: What? Could you not watch one hour with me?

meditations.body: One hour. Every holy hour ever kept began as this reproach.

scripture.text: Watch ye: and pray that ye enter not into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh weak.

meditations.body: Look at what He does with their failure. He is in the worst hour of His life; He asked for one thing; they slept through it. And His response is to excuse them while asking again — the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh weak. He supplies, mid-agony, the gentlest available reading of the men who let Him down. It is worth holding this beside how you narrate the failures of the people who have disappointed you, and the failures you confess of yourself. His diagnosis is accurate and it is kind, at the same time, about the same weakness.

scripture.text: In thy sight are all they that afflict me; my heart hath expected reproach and misery. And I looked for one that would grieve together with me, but there was none: and for one that would comfort me, and I found none.

meditations.body: The psalm describes this night with an accuracy that aches: He looked for a companion in grief and found none. He wanted watchers. He asked for them by name, three of them, and asked twice more. If the Lord Himself, facing His Passion, gathered company for His prayer — whom have you asked to watch with you in yours? The saints and the angels are not too busy. Asking them is not weakness. It is the imitation of Christ in Gethsemani.

scripture.text: Jesus therefore said to Peter: Put up thy sword into the scabbard. The chalice which my father hath given me, shall I not drink it?

meditations.body: Marmion points to the change in grammar. In the garden, the chalice was a petition: let it pass. Minutes later, at the arrest, it has become a rhetorical question that expects no answer: shall I not drink it? Between the two sentences lies the whole agony — and after it, Marmion says, He will go to the very end in His sacrifice. The struggle was real and it was finished. He does not renegotiate at the sight of the torches. What was settled kneeling stays settled standing.

scripture.text: Surely he hath borne our infirmities and carried our sorrows: and we have thought him as it were a leper, and as one struck by God and afflicted.

meditations.body: Marmion teaches that in accepting the cross Christ accepted it for all His members, for each one of us — and united to His own sufferings all the sufferings of His mystical body, causing them, in Marmion's phrase, to find in this union their value and price. Which means the agony in the garden had your worst night inside it, and the union runs both directions: what you are carrying can be placed into what He carried, and it stops being waste. Nothing offered there is ever merely endured.

scripture.text: And he saith: Abba, Father, all things are possible to thee: remove this chalice from me; but not what I will, but what thou wilt.

meditations.body: Mark alone keeps the Aramaic word: Abba. In the hour when the request will be refused, the address does not change — it is still the child's word, the intimate name. He says all things are possible to thee, asks, and is not granted, and nothing in the relationship moves an inch. This is the mystery's answer to the hardest question about unanswered prayer: refusal and love are not opposites. The proof is that the refused petition and the word Abba live in the same sentence.

scripture.text: Rise: let us go. Behold he is at hand that will betray me.

meditations.body: The agony ends in a decision and a movement: rise, let us go. He does not wait to be found; He walks toward the torches. And Faber marks what happened at that same hour to the one watching in spirit: the curtain falls, the vision grows dim, and she is left for a while to the anguish of uncertainty. For Him, the clarity of action; for her, the dark of not knowing — the two shapes every surrendered will eventually learns. The decade ends walking, with Him, toward what has been accepted.

scripture.text: Then therefore Pilate took Jesus and scourged him.

meditations.body: Seven words in English, and the Gospel moves on. No adjectives, no description, no count of the blows — the evangelists, who were writing for people who had seen Roman scourging, did not need to explain, and would not linger. The restraint of the text is itself instruction: this mystery is not entered by imagining harder, but by staying longer. Stand in the courtyard for the length of the decade. The sentence is short. The scourging was not.

scripture.text: I have given my body to the strikers, and my cheeks to them that plucked them: I have not turned away my face from them that rebuked me, and spit upon me.

meditations.body: I have given. The verb is active. Nothing was taken that was not first handed over.

scripture.text: The wicked have wrought upon my back: they have lengthened their iniquity.

meditations.body: Faber places His mother in the street outside the praetorium, and gives her the sense that cannot be shut: she hears the sound of the scourging. She hears, he says, the gentle murmurs, the almost inaudible bleatings of her spotless Lamb — she hears them, and omnipotence commands her still to live. Whoever has stood outside a hospital room door, hearing what they could not stop and could not leave, has stood where she stood. She did not run from the sound. She let it reach her, and offered what it did to her.

scripture.text: Then he released to them Barabbas: and having scourged Jesus, delivered him unto them to be crucified.

meditations.body: One verse holds the whole economy of the Passion in miniature: the guilty man walks free, and the innocent one takes the scourge. Barabbas — a convicted insurrectionist and murderer — goes home, and no Gospel records that he said a word. The Church has never been able to read his name without seeing her own. The exchange at the pillar is the exchange of the whole Redemption, performed first in a courtroom: he goes free because Christ stands in his place. So do you.

scripture.text: But he was wounded for our iniquities, he was bruised for our sins: the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his bruises we are healed.

meditations.body: Marmion observes that no mystery of Jesus was announced beforehand with so much care as the Passion — the Psalmist and the prophets laid out its circumstances centuries in advance, and Christ is visibly attentive, all through the Gospel accounts, to fulfil what was written, down to the last detail. Nothing in it is little or negligible, Marmion says, because these are the actions of a God-Man. The scourge was in Isaias seven hundred years before it was in the soldier's hand. What happened at the pillar was not the plan going wrong. It was the plan.

scripture.text: Who his own self bore our sins in his body upon the tree: that we, being dead to sins, should live to justice: by whose stripes you were healed.

meditations.body: By whose stripes you were healed. Peter — who was in the city that night, and hiding — chose the strangest possible word for what the stripes do. Not appalled, not avenged: healed. The wounds are medicine. Injury absorbed with perfect love stops spreading and starts repairing, and the place where the harm landed becomes the place the healing comes from. Somewhere in your own history is a wound of His with your name on its healing.

scripture.text: My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands.

meditations.body: The Church has long seen the scourged Christ in this verse — white and red, innocence and blood, the two colors of the pillar. Denis the Carthusian adds a gloss of his own: He is called white, Denis says, because He is gentle, sweet and kind to the just, above all in rewarding them; and ruddy because He is terrible to the obstinate wicked — for the angry grow red in the face. At the pillar both meanings are literal at once. The gentleness and the fire are the same Beloved, and the beloved is chosen out of thousands.

scripture.text: And he took the blood and sprinkled it upon the people, and he said: This is the blood of the covenant, which the Lord hath made with you concerning all these words.

meditations.body: Faber records a detail from her vantage that is easy to hurry past: she sees the people around Him sprinkled with His Blood. Bystanders and soldiers walked out of that courtyard carrying the Precious Blood on their clothes and skin, unasked and unaware. The scene remembers Sinai, where Moses sprinkled the blood of the covenant on the people — except that this time the blood is God's own, and the people being sprinkled are the ones shedding it. The new covenant's first sprinkling fell on the guilty, which is the only kind of people it was ever for.

scripture.text: I will chastise him therefore and release him.

meditations.body: Pilate's compromise: torture the man I have just declared innocent, to appease the men who want him dead. It satisfied no one, as compromises with a mob never do.

scripture.text: And all the multitude sought to touch him: for virtue went out from him and healed all.

meditations.body: Marmion asks why meditating on the Passion does so much in a soul. When Christ walked the earth, virtue went out from Him and healed all who touched Him — and that virtue, Marmion says, still goes out. Christ is not a dead and inert model: ever living, He produces in those who draw near in faith the very perfection they contemplate in His Person. This decade is not remembering. It is contact.

scripture.text: But I, as a deaf man, heard not: and as a dumb man not opening his mouth. And I became as a man that heareth not: and that hath no reproofs in his mouth.

meditations.body: No Gospel records a single word from Him at the pillar. He who answered Pilate, who will speak seven times from the cross, says nothing here at all. The psalm had described it: as a dumb man, not opening his mouth. There are sufferings that are meant to be protested and sufferings that are meant to be offered, and the wisdom to tell them apart is one of the harder gifts to ask for. His silence at the pillar was not weakness or shock. It was the most expensive thing in the courtyard, and it was chosen.

scripture.text: Yet so, that they exceed not the number of forty: lest thy brother depart shamefully torn before thy eyes.

meditations.body: The Law of Moses set a mercy-limit on flogging: forty stripes and no more, lest thy brother depart shamefully torn — even punishment must not unmake a man's dignity. Rome scourged, and Rome had no such verse. Handed to Gentile power, He stood outside the protection His own Law had written for the least of His brothers. The One who gave the mercy-limit on Sinai received a punishment that had none. He knew the statute. He was its author. He let it not apply to Him.

scripture.text: Who now rejoice in my sufferings for you and fill up those things that are wanting of the sufferings of Christ, in my flesh, for his body, which is the church:

meditations.body: Paul says something at first hearing impossible: that anything could be wanting in the sufferings of Christ. Nothing is lacking in their worth — the pillar alone could redeem worlds. What remains unfinished is the Passion's arrival in each member of His body, and Paul rejoices that his own flesh is one of the places it lands. Yours is another. So the question this decade leaves open on purpose: what suffering are you carrying that has not yet been offered — still merely happening to you, when it could be joined to Him?

scripture.text: For the foolishness of God is wiser than men: and the weakness of God is stronger than men.

meditations.body: Consider what the courtyard looked like to everyone in it. Soldiers saw routine work. Pilate saw a political instrument. The crowd saw a failed prophet getting what failed prophets get. Not one eye present could see that the turning point of the world was passing through that yard — that the weakness on display was strength of a kind the empire had no category for. Most of God's decisive work looks, at the time, like defeat being administered to somebody. It is worth remembering on the days your own faithfulness looks to you like losing.

scripture.text: From the sole of the foot unto the top of the head, there is no soundness therein: wounds and bruises and swelling sores: they are not bound up, nor dressed, nor fomented with oil.

meditations.body: Isaias wrote it of a sinful nation; the Church reads it over the sinless body at the pillar: from the sole of the foot to the top of the head, no soundness — and the wounds not bound up, nor dressed, nor fomented with oil. No one tended Him. They untied Him and moved on to the next thing. Let the decade end there, in the pause the Gospels do not record: the courtyard emptying, the pillar dark, and the wounds undressed — because the dressing of those wounds was always going to be ours to do, in the least of His brethren, wherever we find them untended.

scripture.text: Despised, and the most abject of men, a man of sorrows, and acquainted with infirmity: and his look was as it were hidden and despised, whereupon we esteemed him not.

meditations.body: Velazquez painted this decade. Christ sits bound at the fallen pillar, the scourges on the ground, and to the side kneels a child — the Christian soul — with an angel's hand on its shoulder, being taught simply to look. Nothing in the picture moves. Be the child now. Do not analyse, do not resolve; let His mother's way of seeing become yours for a moment — not the horror, but the sorrow, and the love underneath it that chose this for you. And before you rise to the next mystery, answer Him one thing, silently, in your own words: what will you leave here at the pillar with Him tonight?

scripture.text: Then the soldiers of the governor, taking Jesus into the hall, gathered together unto him the whole band.

meditations.body: They gathered the whole band — an audience assembled on purpose. The scourging was a sentence; this is entertainment. Soldiers far from home, bored and brutal, given an hour with a condemned man whose charge sheet says king. What follows is theater: costume, crown, sceptre, homage, all of it staged for laughter. Enter the hall and stay for the decade. Everything they do in mockery, you are about to do in earnest, and the difference between their hour and yours is the whole meaning of worship.

scripture.text: And they clothed him with purple: and, platting a crown of thorns, they put it upon him.

meditations.body: Faber saw the scene through her eyes: she has beheld, he says, the ruffians in the guard-room celebrate the cruel coronation of the Almighty King. Coronation is his word, and it is exact. Every element of a true crowning is present — the robe, the diadem, the sceptre, the acclamation, the bended knee — assembled by men who thought they were inventing a joke. Heaven let them proceed, because the joke was true. He is the King. They crowned Him. The ceremony counts.

scripture.text: And they came to him and said: Hail, king of the Jews. And they gave him blows.

meditations.body: The same sentence holds the salute and the blow. Every Hail Mary of this decade answers that Hail.

scripture.text: Go forth, ye daughters of Sion, and see king Solomon in the diadem, wherewith his mother crowned him in the day of his espousals, and in the day of the joy of his heart.

meditations.body: The Church has always read this verse toward this mystery, and Denis the Carthusian gives its gentlest meaning first. The diadem His mother set on Him is the humanity itself — the flesh the eternal Word took from Mary. A crown, Denis says, because in that nature the whole kindness and generosity of God shine out and are declared. The day of His espousals is the hour of the Incarnation, when the Son of God wedded our nature. And the verse insists it was the day of the joy of His heart. Before any thorns, He was crowned by Mary — with us.

scripture.text: But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour: that, through the grace of God he might taste death for all.

meditations.body: Then Denis turns the verse over. The mother who crowned Him can also be read as the Synagogue, of whom He was born according to the flesh — and her crown was the Passion. But watch where Denis takes it: by bearing that crowning with perfect charity, obedience, and patience, Christ merited another. Denis seals it with the apostle's words: we see Jesus, for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour. Two crowns, then. The one pressed on in mockery purchased the one set on in glory — and He is never pictured in heaven without the scars of the first.

scripture.text: Thorns and thistles shall it bring forth to thee, and thou shalt eat the herbs of the earth.

meditations.body: Thorns enter Scripture on the day of the Fall — the ground's answer to Adam's sin, the first visible form the curse took. They have no other origin story. So when the soldiers reached for the nearest thornbush to make their joke, they were handling, without knowing it, the oldest artifact of the ruin Christ had come to repair. He wears the curse of Adam's ground braided onto His head. The second Adam is crowned with the harvest of the first, and carries it out the door toward the tree that undoes the tree.

scripture.text: His eyes shall see the king in his beauty, they shall see the land far off.

meditations.body: Faber lets two details from the guard-room stand without softening: she has seen the eyes of the All-seeing bandaged, and the offscouring of the people bending the knee in derision before Him who will one day pronounce their doom. The blindfold is the mystery in miniature — creatures covering the eyes that made light, then asking who struck the blow. The knee is its double: the gesture correct, the heart inverted. Every posture in that room will be repeated at the end of time with the irony removed. Some of those knees will bend again.

scripture.text: And as he was yet speaking, behold a bright cloud overshadowed them. And lo a voice out of the cloud, saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased: hear ye him.

meditations.body: Marmion makes the claim that holds this whole mystery together: the Father contemplates His Son with love not only on Thabor, when Christ stands in the splendour of His glory, but likewise when Pilate shows Him to the multitude, crowned with thorns and become the outcast of humanity — this is my beloved Son applies equally in both scenes. The delight of the Father did not flicker when the face was disfigured. If you pray the Luminous mysteries, you will stand on Thabor and hear the voice; stand here first and know it is saying the same thing.

scripture.text: (Jesus therefore came forth, bearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment.) And he saith to them: Behold the Man.

meditations.body: Faber hears Pilate's words as testimony given unawares: there was need, he says, that someone should testify He was man — for one who was only man could never have survived the crushing of the winepress, the threefold pressure of His Father, of demons, and of men. Behold the Man: still standing under a weight assembled from every direction at once. The governor meant it as an appeal to pity. The Church has kept it as a title, because no truer sentence was spoken in the praetorium.

scripture.text: But I am a worm, and no man: the reproach of men, and the outcast of the people.

meditations.body: The psalm He will pray from the cross had already described the balcony: the reproach of men, and the outcast of the people.

scripture.text: But they cried out: Away with him: Away with him: Crucify him. Pilate saith to them: shall I crucify your king? The chief priests answered: We have no king but Caesar.

meditations.body: Then, Faber writes, rose over the piazza that wild yell of blasphemous rejection which still rings in our ears — and dwells, he adds, even in that calm heaven above, in the Mother's ear who heard it in all the savage frightfulness of its reality. She was in the crowd when the crowd chose. Voices that had cried Hosanna five days earlier now priced her Son below Caesar. Faber's point is not the crowd's fickleness but her hearing: some sounds are not survived so much as carried, and she carried that one into glory.

scripture.text: For which cause, God also hath exalted him and hath given him a name which is above all names: That in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those that are in heaven, on earth, and under the earth:

meditations.body: Denis, in the passage where he lets Mary herself speak the Canticle verse, has her say the diadem is the humanity He took from me — and then he reaches for exactly this text: He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming obedient even to the death of the cross; for which cause God hath exalted Him, and given Him the name above every name. The soldiers' knees bent first, in derision — and Paul says every knee will bend at the last, in truth. The mockery of the guard-room was an accidental rehearsal of the liturgy of heaven.

scripture.text: Who, when he was reviled, did not revile: when he suffered, he threatened not, but delivered himself to him that judged him unjustly.

meditations.body: Through the whole pantomime — the robe, the reed, the spitting, the hailing — He says nothing at all. Peter, who knew Him, marked it as the thing to imitate: when He was reviled, He did not revile. Mockery is the one suffering that begs for a comeback; it hands you the script and waits. He declined the script. His kingship needed no defending because it was not in question — only invisible. The next time ridicule hands you its script, you will know what royalty does with it.

scripture.text: And Herod with his army set him at nought and mocked him, putting on him a white garment: and sent him back to Pilate.

meditations.body: It happened twice. Herod's men dressed Him in white for a fool; Pilate's men dressed Him in purple for a king. Two courts, two costumes, one joke — and both costumes told the truth the costumers could not see: He is the spotless one, and He is the King. The world has only ever had two ways to dismiss Christ, as madman or as pretender, and both were fitted onto Him as garments in a single morning. Which of the two dismissals do you hear more often — and had you noticed that both required dressing Him up first?

scripture.text: And after they had mocked him, they took off the cloak from him and put on him his own garments and led him away to crucify him.

meditations.body: Read the verse slowly: they took off the cloak — the Gospel is explicit — and put on Him His own garments. Of the crown, not a word. Scripture never records its removal, and the Church's art has always painted Him carrying the cross crowned, and crucified crowned. The joke was over; the coronation was not. He walked out of the praetorium wearing it, and He wears its scars in glory now. The decade ends at the door: the King, crowned by us, going out to win the kingdom.

scripture.text: And he shall grow up as a tender plant before him, and as a root out of a thirsty ground: there is no beauty in him, nor comeliness: and we have seen him, and there was no sightliness, that we should be desirous of him:

meditations.body: Faber, watching her watch Him on the balcony, reaches for an impossible pair of words: beautiful in His disfigurement. Isaias had said there would be no beauty in Him, no sightliness — and both are true, because the beauty is not in what was done to the Face but in why it was borne. So end the decade the way she ended it: not analysing, not resolving, only gazing. Let the crowned Face fill the whole field of your attention, the way an icon does, and let it look back at you with the eyes they bandaged. Every heart crowns Him with something — trust or thorns, and often both in one day. What have your hands woven for Him this week?

scripture.text: And bearing his own cross, he went forth to the place which is called Calvary, but in Hebrew Golgotha.

meditations.body: Four words in the middle of the verse: bearing his own cross. The instrument of the execution is laid on the condemned, which was Roman practice and is also the whole shape of the thing — He carries what will kill Him, through streets filled with people who have come out to watch. Somewhere along that route His mother is standing at a corner, waiting for the procession to reach her. Stand with her while it comes.

scripture.text: Mem. To what shall I compare thee? or to what shall I liken thee, O daughter of Jerusalem? to what shall I equal thee, that I may comfort thee, O virgin daughter of Sion? for great as the sea is thy destruction: who shall heal thee?

meditations.body: St Bernardine, whom Liguori quotes at the head of his discourse, makes the measure absolute: all the sorrows of the world together would not equal the sorrow of Mary. The reasoning is not rhetoric. To weigh a mother's grief you must first weigh her love, and this mother's heart and her Son's heart, as she told St Bridget, were one heart. The fire of that love did not go out at the Passion. It became, in Liguori's phrase, a sea of sorrow — the same magnitude, converted.

scripture.text: He was offered because it was his own will, and he opened not his mouth: he shall be led as a sheep to the slaughter, and shall be dumb as a lamb before his shearer, and he shall not open his mouth.

meditations.body: Because it was his own will. The sentence was Pilate's; the consent was not.

scripture.text: Beth. Weeping, she hath wept in the night, and her tears are on her cheeks: there is none to comfort her among all them that were dear to her: all her friends have despised her, and are become her enemies.

meditations.body: Liguori reconstructs her night from the saints' testimony. St Bonaventure says she spent it without sleep — while the others slept, she watched. And in the morning the disciples began arriving at her door, one after another, each carrying a different piece of the same news: the treatment in the house of Caiphas, the mockery before Herod, and at last John himself, with word that Pilate had passed the sentence. She learned the Passion the way the poor always learn catastrophe — in fragments, from messengers, each knock worse than the last.

scripture.text: Before the festival day of the pasch, Jesus knowing that his hour was come, that he should pass out of this world to the Father: having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them unto the end.

meditations.body: The Virgin told St Bridget, as Liguori reports it, that in the days when the Passion drew near her eyes were always filled with tears, and a cold sweat covered her from the fear of what was coming. Then the appointed day came, and Jesus came to her in tears to take His leave before going to death. The Gospels record His farewells to the disciples at length. His farewell to her they leave in silence, and the saints have filled that silence with reverent conjecture ever since — because there is no version of that hour that is easy to imagine.

scripture.text: And taking bread, he gave thanks and brake and gave to them, saying: This is my body, which is given for you. Do this for a commemoration of me.

meditations.body: Faber asks where she found the strength to go out and meet Him, and his answer is the boldest stroke in the chapter. She had received the Blessed Sacrament the night before, and He was still within her — she carried Him, in a strange sense, as Viaticum, and went to meet Him condemned. Then the sentence that deserves a lifetime of chewing: it is only with Jesus that any of us can meet Jesus. What carried her through that street is what carries you back from the altar rail.

scripture.text: Lamed. O all ye that pass by the way, attend, and see if there be any sorrow like to my sorrow: for he hath made a vintage of me, as the Lord spoke in the day of his fierce anger.

meditations.body: Faber slows the meeting itself down to single gestures. The procession reaches her corner. He halts. He lifts the one hand that is free and clears the blood from His eyes — and Faber will not let you misread the motion: not so that He can see her. So that she can see Him. His last service to His mother before Calvary is to make sure that when she looks, she meets His eyes and not only His wounds.

scripture.text: And as they led him away, they laid hold of one Simon of Cyrene, coming from the country; and they laid the cross on him to carry after Jesus.

meditations.body: A man walking into the city on other business, conscripted at sword-point into the Gospel.

scripture.text: For I am ready for scourges: and my sorrow is continually before me.

meditations.body: She approaches to embrace Him, and the soldiers thrust her back — His mother, Faber says, and she reeled with the push and then was still. Then she watches Him go down under the weight of the cross, the sound of it, the men around Him dragging Him up again. He is her Babe of Bethlehem, Faber writes, and she is helpless, and cannot get near, and omnipotence held her heart fast. There is a suffering in being kept from helping that is its own entire category, and every parent of a suffering child knows its taste.

scripture.text: And thy own soul a sword shall pierce, that, out of many hearts thoughts may be revealed.

meditations.body: Faber notes what kind of sorrow this one was: the arrival of an evil long foreseen. She had carried Simeon's sentence for thirty-three years. And then he writes a page that could have been written this morning, about what he calls the unpreparedness of extreme preparation — how we rehearse the dreaded thing, imagine every circumstance, practise the attitude in which we will receive the blow. And then it comes, and observes not one of our rubrics: wrong road, wrong hour, wrong weapon, wrong place. Knowing it was coming turns out to be no protection at all.

scripture.text: But Jesus turning to them, said: Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not over me; but weep for yourselves and for your children.

meditations.body: The only words the Gospels record from Him on the whole road, and they are a correction of the crowd's tears. The women weep over Him as a spectacle of pity, and He turns — carrying the cross, He turns — to redirect their weeping toward what actually needs it. It is worth asking of your own compassion where it goes. Is it spent on the sufferings it is comfortable to weep over, or on the ones He would point you toward?

scripture.text: Put me as a seal upon thy heart, as a seal upon thy arm, for love is strong as death, jealousy as hard as hell, the lamps thereof are fire and flames.

meditations.body: St Lawrence Justinian, in Liguori's citation, compresses the whole economy of her suffering into one clause: the more tenderly she loved, the more deeply she was wounded. There is no route to loving much that does not widen the surface where grief can land. She had the greatest love that any creature has borne, and therefore the greatest exposure — and she did not, on that account, love less. That is the choice this decade puts to anyone who has considered loving more carefully in order to suffer less.

scripture.text: And the peace of God, which surpasseth all understanding, keep your hearts and minds in Christ Jesus.

meditations.body: Faber records something in her that no one would predict: as the procession drew near, the peace of her heart grew deeper. It could not help it, he says — God was approaching, and peace went before Him. The anguish was unutterable and the peace was real, at the same time, in the same heart. Anyone who has kept vigil at a deathbed of someone they loved in God may recognise this from the inside. The two do not cancel. They coexist.

scripture.text: And he said to all: If any man will come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.

meditations.body: He said this a long time before Jerusalem, and on this road it stops being a metaphor. Daily is the word to sit with. Not once, heroically, at some future crisis you half look forward to — daily, which means the cross is mostly made of ordinary material: the same person to forgive again, the same work, the same body, the same street. She followed Him up the actual road. The daily version is the one handed to you.

scripture.text: Teth. The Lord is good to them that hope in him, to the soul that seeketh him. Teth. It is good to wait with silence for the salvation of God.

meditations.body: Liguori set this verse over his whole discourse on the meeting. She could not stop the procession, could not carry the cross, could not even stay at His side — the soldiers saw to that. What remained to her was to follow slowly behind, in a peace past man's understanding, with Magdalen and John leaning their broken hearts on hers. Sometimes the whole of faithfulness is reduced to that: you cannot help, you cannot fix, you can only refuse to leave. She walked the rest of the road. So can you.

scripture.text: And when they were come to the place which is called Calvary, they crucified him there: and the robbers, one on the right hand, and the other on the left.

meditations.body: It is a little before noon when they reach the top of the hill. Faber passes on the old tradition that this was the site of Adam's grave — the new Adam lifted up over the bones of the first. Whether or not the tradition is true, the Church has always known what it means: the tree is planted where the ruin began. You have five decades' worth of Hail Marys to stand on this hill. Do not hurry to leave it.

scripture.text: Now there stood by the cross of Jesus, his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalen.

meditations.body: Liguori notices the economy of the verse: there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother — and St John says nothing more, because nothing more can be said. Behold her at the foot of the cross, looking on her dying Son, and then see if there is grief like her grief. And she told St Bridget the one detail John left out: I did not leave him, and I stood nearer to his cross. When the executioners finished their work and stepped back, she stepped forward.

scripture.text: For many dogs have encompassed me: the council of the malignant hath besieged me. They have dug my hands and feet. They have numbered all my bones. And they have looked and stared upon me.

meditations.body: David wrote the description a thousand years before the Romans invented the method.

scripture.text: Strength and beauty are her clothing, and she shall laugh in the latter day.

meditations.body: St Bonaventure, in Liguori's citation, puts the hard question to her directly: why did you go to Calvary at all? Should not shame have kept you away — or at least the horror of seeing God crucified by His own creatures? Then the saint answers for her, in five Latin words worth memorizing: thy heart did not consider the horror, but the sorrow. She was not looking at what the scene was. She was looking at what He was suffering. William the Abbot adds the verdict: a true mother, whom not even the terror of death could separate from her Son.

scripture.text: And when the sixth hour was come, there was darkness over the whole earth until the ninth hour.

meditations.body: Faber does the arithmetic no one else thinks to do: barely four hours separate the meeting in the street from the moment of His death — the procession reached the summit a little before noon, and the ninth hour, three in the afternoon, ended it. Four hours, against the eighteen years of Nazareth. And yet, he says, in sorrow and in sanctification those hours are the longer epoch: in nothing is it more true than in our sanctification that with God a thousand years are as one day. Holiness is not measured by the clock but by the depth at which love meets God in what is happening. There are afternoons that do the work of decades. Perhaps you have had one.

scripture.text: Caph. My eyes have failed with weeping, my bowels are troubled: my liver is poured out upon the earth, for the destruction of the daughter of my people, when the children, and the sucklings, fainted away in the streets of the city.

meditations.body: Liguori assembles the Fathers on what was happening in her while it happened in Him. St Jerome: every torture inflicted on the body of Jesus was a wound in the heart of the mother. St John Chrysostom: anyone on Calvary that day would have seen two altars — one in the body of Jesus, one in the heart of Mary. And Bonaventure corrects even that: not two altars. One. The cross alone, on which, with the divine Lamb, the mother also was sacrificed.

scripture.text: For I, through the law, am dead to the law, that I may live to God; with Christ I am nailed to the cross.

meditations.body: St Bernard, as Liguori relays him, preserves a detail from which the mind flinches: the nails were not sharp, but blunt — non acutis, sed obtusis. And St Augustine draws the conclusion about her: the cross and nails of the Son were also the cross and nails of the mother; Christ being crucified, the mother was crucified too. Paul claims the same crucifixion for every Christian — with Christ I am nailed to the cross — and she is the proof that it can be true of a person standing on the ground with unmarked hands.

scripture.text: And he said to Jesus: Lord, remember me when thou shalt come into thy kingdom. And Jesus said to him: Amen I say to thee: This day thou shalt be with me in paradise.

meditations.body: Faber says that sorrow widens great hearts, just as it contracts little ones — and his evidence is what she did with hers on Calvary. She had taken the two thieves for sons. She was, in his startling phrase, greedy of children. She wrestled in prayer for both of them, and when grace broke open the heart of one, answered prayer only made her more covetous: she counted Dismas as a beginning, and pleaded harder for the other. Watch what her grief did. It did not close her. It annexed two criminals.

scripture.text: And one of those robbers who were hanged blasphemed him, saying: If thou be Christ, save thyself and us.

meditations.body: Faber's account of the other thief is the most terrible page in his chapter. Graces descended on him like flights of angels — they fluttered at his heart, sang for entrance, made it bleed with remorse. But it was its own master. It would not open. So near Jesus, and to be lost — his face beside the face of Christ, the Precious Blood strewn around him — and by his own will detached from the very side of the Crucifix. Heaven did not resist him. He resisted heaven. It is the one power that was never taken from any of us.

scripture.text: The Lord is nigh unto them that are of a contrite heart: and he will save the humble of spirit.

meditations.body: In the middle of the scene Faber stops and asks a question he does not answer, and neither will this meditation: is it that Jesus breaks the hearts over which He reigns, or that He comes of special choice to reign in broken hearts? Sit with it for the length of the decade. Your own history with Him is part of the evidence.

scripture.text: When Jesus therefore had seen his mother and the disciple standing whom he loved, he saith to his mother: Woman, behold thy son. After that, he saith to the disciple: Behold thy mother. And from that hour, the disciple took her to his own.

meditations.body: A dying man's words are few and expensive, and He spends a whole sentence on this. He has nothing left to bequeath — they have His garments already, at the foot of the cross — so He gives away the only two possessions remaining: His mother to the disciple, the disciple to His mother. The Church has always heard more than John's name in that word. The disciple standing there is the one He loved; so is the one praying this decade. From that hour, she is yours too.

scripture.text: Afterwards, Jesus knowing that all things were now accomplished, that the scripture might be fulfilled, said: I thirst.

meditations.body: Two words. The one who made the sea asks His creatures for a drink, and is given vinegar.

scripture.text: Put me as a seal upon thy heart, as a seal upon thy arm, for love is strong as death, jealousy as hard as hell, the lamps thereof are fire and flames.

meditations.body: Denis the Carthusian hears this verse spoken between the crucified Son and His mother. She pressed Him and all His mysteries — all His love for us, and His most bitter Passion — into her heart indelibly, and inscribed them there, he says, in letters of blood. And ever afterward she kept turning that inscription over: to grieve with Him, to imitate, to give thanks, to marvel, to love, to contemplate. What you are doing in this decade — holding the Passion in mind on purpose — is the thing she did first, and never stopped doing. In her the love was, as the verse says, strong as death; for it she counted everything on earth as nothing.

scripture.text: And about the ninth hour, Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying: Eli, Eli, lamma sabacthani? That is, My God, My God, why hast thou forsaken me?

meditations.body: The most terrible sentence in the Gospels is a quotation. It is the first line of the psalm in which David describes pierced hands and divided garments — a psalm every Jew on that hill knew entire, and which does not end in abandonment but in vindication: all the ends of the earth shall remember, and shall be converted to the Lord. He is praying, aloud, with the last of His breath, the prayer of a forsaken man — and the prayer itself already contains the far side. When your own prayer can manage nothing but the first line of a psalm, the rest of the psalm still stands.

scripture.text: Jesus therefore, when he had taken the vinegar, said: It is consummated. And bowing his head, he gave up the ghost.

meditations.body: Liguori taught, back at the Presentation, that when she offered her forty-day-old Son in the temple she knew the sacrifice would one day be consummated upon the altar of the cross. This is that day, and the word from the cross is the same word: consummated. The offering she began with pigeons in her hands, thirty-three years ago, is complete. And she is still standing — the verse before this one put her there and nothing has moved her. The decade ends where she is: upright, at the foot of it, having withheld nothing. Stay a moment before the next mystery. It is finished, and she has not left.

scripture.text: And again another scripture saith: They shall look on him whom they pierced.

meditations.body: Denis the Carthusian hears one of the Canticle's strangest lines — under the apple tree I raised thee up — as Christ speaking to His own mother: by the tree of the cross He redeemed even her, the grace of Calvary reaching backward to the first instant of her existence, centuries before the Church found words for what that implies. The work is that finished. It runs forward to you and backward to her, and nothing is outside it. So end the way the Scripture ends the scene: they shall look on him whom they pierced. Only look — at the stillness after the sixth word, the work complete, nothing left undone. And take one question into the silence: what in you is still trying to finish what He has already finished?
